title: Final mock interview and capstone
goal: Prove it under interview conditions: three whiteboard scripts, one final bug hunt, 30 rapid-fire questions, 6 troubleshooting scenarios, and the final checklist.
setup: # W1: a small access log (combined format, one broken line)
# W3: a list of URLs to check, and a tiny site
# P4: the take-home script with bugs from all four weeks

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# take-home.sh: for each path in paths.txt print "path: <path>" exactly as written,' '# count the lines of access.log that have status 500 or 503,' '# and append one summary line per run to summary.log. Exit 1 if access.log is missing.' 'LOG=access.log' 'if [-f $LOG]; then echo "log found"; else echo "no log"; exit 1; fi' 'while read p; do echo "path: $p"; done < paths.txt' 'count_errors() { return $(grep -cE " 50[03] " $LOG); }' 'count_errors' 'ERRORS=$?' 'echo "$(date +%F) errors=$ERRORS" > summary.log' 'echo "errors: $ERRORS"' > take-home.sh

warmup.q: How does a shell step tell Jenkins it failed?
warmup.a: With a non-zero exit code. Nothing else counts.

warmup.q: Which exit codes do Nagios-style checks use?
What is the order of checks when you cannot SSH to a server?
warmup.a: Name (DNS), then port/network (`nc -zv host 22`), then key, user and permissions, then `ssh -v` and the server's auth log.

problems.title: Whiteboard 1: top IPs that got server errors
problems.situation: Interviewer: "Write a script that takes an Nginx access log and prints the N client IPs that received the most 5xx errors. Handle bad input." Write it on paper first (8 minutes), then type and test it.
task: Usage: `top-errors.sh LOGFILE [N]`, N defaults to 3. Wrong usage → message to stderr, exit 2.
If the file cannot be read → error, exit 1.
Parse robustly (split at the quotes), keep only 5xx, count per IP, biggest first, top N.
Test: normal run, `N=1`, a missing file, and no arguments.
solution: # Usage: top-errors.sh LOGFILE [N]   - top N client IPs by number of 5xx responses
[[ $N =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "error: N must be a number" >&2; exit 2; }

explanation.meaning: Safe defaults: say this out loud in the interview (Day 22).
Different codes for wrong usage and runtime errors (Day 6).
Robust parsing of combined logs; field 1 starts with the IP (Day 23).
The counting pipeline (Day 12).
Quote every variable (Day 5).

problems.expected_output:
5 10.0.0.5
      3 172.16.0.3
      3 10.0.0.7
exit code: 0
      5 10.0.0.5
exit code: 0
error: cannot read nope.log
exit code: 1
usage: top-errors.sh LOGFILE [N]
exit code: 2
mistakes: Writing the pipeline but no input checks: interviewers want to see usage messages and exit codes.
Using `$9` for the status: mention why splitting at quotes is safer.
problems.interview_say: I start with set -euo pipefail, check the arguments and the file, parse the log by splitting at the quotes, filter 5xx, then count with sort, uniq -c, sort -rn and head. Bad usage exits 2, a missing file exits 1.
problems.try_yourself: Add a `-s CODE` option to count one exact status code instead of all 5xx.

problems.title: Whiteboard 2: back up a folder, keep the last 3
problems.situation: Interviewer: "Write a backup script for a folder: a timestamped tar.gz, keep only the last 3 backups, and fail clearly if something goes wrong." The answer stays short and correct; extras (checksum, S3, lock) can be mentioned at the end.
task: Usage: `backup-keep.sh SRC DEST [KEEP]`, KEEP defaults to 3.
Create `DEST/NAME-YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS.tar.gz` (allow `STAMP` from the environment for tests).
Delete all but the newest KEEP backups of that source.
Test with 5 runs (different STAMPs), then show what is left. Test a missing source.
solution: SRC=${1:?usage: backup-keep.sh SRC DEST [KEEP]}; DEST=${2:?usage: backup-keep.sh SRC DEST [KEEP]}; KEEP=${3:-3}
[ -d "$SRC" ] || { echo "error: $SRC is not a folder" >&2; exit 1; }
bash backup-keep.sh missing-dir backups; echo "exit code: $?"

explanation.meaning: Required arguments with a usage message (Day 13).
Real time normally, fixed time in tests (Day 24).
Pack the folder contents (Day 20).
Keep the newest by name; `-r` = nothing to do is not an error (Day 24).
Checksums, a restore test, a lock (flock), off-site copy to S3, cron with a log, alert on failure.

problems.expected_output:
created app-data-20261016-023000.tar.gz
created app-data-20261017-023000.tar.gz
created app-data-20261018-023000.tar.gz
created app-data-20261019-023000.tar.gz
removed 'backups/app-data-20261016-023000.tar.gz'
created app-data-20261020-023000.tar.gz
removed 'backups/app-data-20261017-023000.tar.gz'
app-data-20261018-023000.tar.gz  app-data-20261020-023000.tar.gz
app-data-20261019-023000.tar.gz
error: missing-dir is not a folder
exit code: 1
mistakes: Rotating with `ls -t`: file times change when backups are copied or restored (Day 24).
Forgetting to mention the restore test: a backup is only good if it can be restored.
problems.interview_say: My backup script makes a timestamped tar.gz, keeps the newest N by sorting the names, and stops on errors with set -e and clear messages. In production I add a checksum, a lock, an S3 copy and a regular restore test.
problems.try_yourself: Add a checksum file for each backup and remove it together with the old archive.

problems.title: Whiteboard 3: check a list of URLs
problems.situation: Interviewer: "We have a file with one URL per line. Write a script that checks each one and reports which are down. It runs in cron, so it must not hang, and the exit code must show if anything is down."
task: Read `urls.txt` line by line, skipping empty lines and comments.
For each URL: `curl -fsS -o /dev/null --max-time 3`, with 2 tries. Print `UP` or `DOWN` and the URL.
At the end print the number of DOWN URLs. Exit 1 if any are down, else 0.
Test against the local test server on port 8151 (one URL points to a closed port).
hints: `while IFS= read -r url; do [[ -z $url || $url == \#* ]] && continue; ... done < "$FILE"`
Count with `DOWN=$((DOWN + 1))`; the loop reads from the file, so the counter survives (Day 8).
solution: # Usage: check-urls.sh URL_FILE   - exit 0 if all URLs are up, 1 if any is down

explanation.meaning: A down URL is expected; the script must check all of them (Day 25).

explanation.part: while IFS= read -r url; ... done < file
explanation.meaning: Safe line reading; the counter is kept (Day 8).
Config files have comments and blank lines (Day 10).
Fail on HTTP errors, never hang (Day 18).
One retry against short glitches (Day 27).
The last command sets the exit code: 0 if none are down, 1 otherwise.

problems.expected_output:
UP    http://127.0.0.1:8151/health.json
UP    http://127.0.0.1:8151/index.html
DOWN  http://127.0.0.1:8151/missing
DOWN  http://127.0.0.1:8159/
down: 2
exit code: 1
mistakes: No timeout: one hanging server blocks the whole cron run.
Reading the file with `for url in $(cat urls.txt)`: comments and spaces break it.
problems.interview_say: I read the URL file with `while IFS= read -r`, skip comments, check each URL with `curl -fsS --max-time` and one retry, print UP or DOWN, and exit 1 if any URL is down so cron or CI can alert.
problems.try_yourself: Check the URLs in parallel with `xargs -P 4` (Day 12). How do you count the DOWN ones then?

problems.title: Final bug hunt: the take-home script
problems.situation: The last task of a take-home test: `take-home.sh` has bugs from all four weeks. The goal is in the comments. Find them by running the script, reading the errors, and reading the code line by line.
task: Run `bash take-home.sh` and compare the output with the comments.
Find 5 bugs: the test brackets, the read options, the function result, the log redirect, and the missing quotes.
Fix them. Run the script twice and show `summary.log`.
hints: The Windows path lost its backslashes: `while IFS= read -r p`.
`return $(grep -c ...)` is an exit code (0-255), and `>` replaces the log each run. Use `echo` + `$( )`, and `>>`.
solution: # take-home.sh: for each path in paths.txt print "path: <path>" exactly as written,
# count the lines of access.log that have status 500 or 503,
# and append one summary line per run to summary.log. Exit 1 if access.log is missing.
if [ -f "$LOG" ]; then echo "log found"; else echo "no log" >&2; exit 1; fi
while IFS= read -r p; do echo "path: $p"; done < paths.txt

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: `[-f` is not a command (Day 6).
Bug 2: `read` without `-r` removed the backslashes of `C:\temp\export` (Day 8).
Bug 3: the count came back as an exit code; with `set -e` that would even stop the script (Day 9).
Bug 4: `>` kept only the last run (Day 4).
Bug 5: unquoted variables; also the pattern now matches the status right after the closing quote, not a size like ` 500 ` (Day 10, Day 23).
Here only to hide the date column, which changes every day.

problems.expected_output:
take-home.sh: line 6: [-f: command not found
no log
--- fixed, run 1 ---
log found
path: C:\temp\export
path: /var/log/todo
errors: 13
--- fixed, run 2 ---
summary.log has 2 lines:
errors=13
errors=13
mistakes: Fixing only the lines that print an error. Bugs 2 to 5 give wrong results without any error message.
Keeping `return` and adding `set -e`: the script then stops after `count_errors` when the count is not 0.
problems.interview_say: I run the script, read the errors, then read every line against the goal. The usual suspects are test syntax, `read -r`, `return` used for data, `>` versus `>>`, and missing quotes. ShellCheck finds several of them automatically.
problems.try_yourself: Run `shellcheck take-home.sh` on the original version (Reset and setup again). Which of the 5 bugs does it find?

interview.q: Rapid 1: Difference between a hard link and a symlink?
interview.a: Hard link: another name for the same data, survives deleting the original, no folders. Symlink: a path to a target, breaks if the target is deleted, works for folders and across disks.

interview.q: Rapid 2: Where are configs, logs and user homes?
interview.a: `/etc`, `/var/log`, `/home`.

interview.q: Rapid 3: Show the last 100 lines of a log and follow it?
interview.a: `tail -n 100 -f app.log` (`-F` if the log rotates).

interview.q: Rapid 4: What does `chmod 640` mean?
interview.a: Owner read+write, group read, others nothing.

interview.q: Rapid 5: Add user `deploy` to group `docker`?
interview.a: `sudo usermod -aG docker deploy` (log in again to apply).

interview.q: Rapid 6: Send stdout and stderr to one file?
interview.a: `cmd > out.log 2>&1` (or `&> out.log`).

interview.q: Rapid 7: What is `/dev/null`?
interview.a: A special file that discards everything written to it.

interview.q: Rapid 8: Single vs double quotes?
interview.a: Single: nothing expands. Double: variables and `$( )` expand, spaces stay together.

interview.q: Rapid 9: What does `export` do?
interview.a: Makes a variable visible to child processes.
`[ ]` is the POSIX test command (quote variables). `[[ ]]` is bash: safe with empty variables, supports patterns and regex.

interview.q: Rapid 11: What does exit code 127 mean?
interview.a: Command not found.

interview.q: Rapid 12: Read a file line by line safely?
interview.a: `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`.

interview.q: Rapid 13: `return` vs `echo` in a function?
interview.a: `return` sets the exit code (0-255); `echo` returns data, captured with `$(func)`.
`"$@"`: each argument separate. `"$*"`: all arguments as one string.

interview.q: Rapid 15: grep options for: ignore case, count, invert, line numbers?
Rapid 16: Replace text in a file in place with a backup?
interview.a: `sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' file`.

interview.q: Rapid 17: Print the 2nd column of a CSV?
interview.a: `awk -F, '{print $2}' file.csv` (or `cut -d, -f2`).

interview.q: Rapid 18: Find files over 100 MB modified more than 30 days ago?
interview.a: `find /path -type f -size +100M -mtime +30`.

interview.q: Rapid 19: Get the file name from a path in bash?
interview.a: `${path##*/}` (folder: `${path%/*}`).

interview.q: Rapid 20: `kill` vs `kill -9`?
interview.a: `kill` sends SIGTERM (clean stop). `kill -9` sends SIGKILL (immediate, no cleanup). TERM first.

interview.q: Rapid 21: The letters in `ps aux`?
interview.a: a = all users, u = user-oriented format, x = also processes without a terminal.

interview.q: Rapid 22: Write a crontab line for every day at 02:30.
interview.a: `30 2 * * * /opt/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1`.

interview.q: Rapid 23: Logs of the systemd service nginx, live?
interview.a: `journalctl -u nginx -f`.

interview.q: Rapid 24: Disk space vs inodes?
interview.a: `df -h` for space, `df -i` for inodes. Either one full gives `No space left on device`.

interview.q: Rapid 25: Which process listens on port 8080?
interview.a: `sudo ss -tulpn | grep :8080` (or `sudo lsof -i :8080`).

interview.q: Rapid 26: curl options for a script-safe health check?
interview.a: `curl -fsS --max-time 5 URL`.

interview.q: Rapid 27: SSH key permissions?
interview.a: `~/.ssh` 700, private key 600, `authorized_keys` 600.

interview.q: Rapid 28: Create and extract a .tar.gz?
interview.a: `tar -czf app.tgz app/` and `tar -xzf app.tgz -C /target`.

interview.q: Rapid 29: What does `set -euo pipefail` do?
interview.a: Exit on errors, error on unset variables, and fail a pipeline if any part fails.

interview.q: Rapid 30: How do you clean up temp files even when a script fails?
interview.a: `TMP=$(mktemp)` plus `trap 'rm -f "$TMP"' EXIT`.

interview.q: Scenario 1: A Kubernetes pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. What do you do?
interview.a: `kubectl describe pod NAME` (events, exit code, OOMKilled?), `kubectl logs NAME --previous` (log of the crashed container), check config/secrets/env and the image tag, then fix and roll out; `kubectl rollout undo` if a new release caused it.

interview.q: Scenario 2: Nginx returns 502 Bad Gateway.
interview.a: Nginx is up but the upstream app is not answering. Check the app (`systemctl status` / pod status), the upstream port with `ss -ltn` and `curl localhost:PORT`, and the Nginx error log (`/var/log/nginx/error.log`: connection refused or timeout).

interview.q: Scenario 3: The Jenkins job fails at `docker push` with "denied" or "unauthorized".
interview.a: Check the registry login (credentials in Jenkins, token expiry), the image name and repository permissions, and whether the repository exists (for example ECR). Run `docker login` in the job with the stored credential.

interview.q: Scenario 4: A cron job did not run last night.
interview.a: Check that cron runs (`systemctl status cron` / `service cron status`), the crontab (`crontab -l`), the syslog (`grep CRON /var/log/syslog`), the job's own log, the PATH and absolute paths, and `%` signs in the crontab line.

interview.q: Scenario 5: The app got slow right after a deploy.
interview.a: Compare before/after: error rate and latency in the logs or metrics, CPU and memory (`top`, `free -m`), database slow queries, and what changed (`git diff` of the release, config). If users suffer, roll back first, investigate second.

interview.q: Scenario 6: Users see a TLS certificate error.
interview.a: Check the expiry date: `echo | openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates`. Renew (for example certbot), check the full chain, reload Nginx, and add an expiry alert.

recap.meaning: First line after the shebang in every script

recap.example: awk -F'"' '{split($3,a," "); print a[1]}' access.log | sort | uniq -c

recap.cmd: while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file
recap.example: while IFS= read -r url; do ...; done < urls.txt
ls -1 b-*.tgz | sort | head -n -3 | xargs -r rm --
echo | openssl s_client -connect site:443 -servername site 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates

checklist: I can explain absolute vs relative paths, and the main folders (/etc, /var/log, /home, /tmp, /usr/bin, /proc).
I can create, copy, move and delete files and folders safely, and explain hard links vs symlinks.
I can read and search logs with head, tail -f, less, grep (with -i -v -c -n -A -B -E -o).
I can read and set permissions with numbers and letters, and explain root vs "others".
I can use >, >>, 2>, 2>&1, /dev/null, pipes, tee and xargs correctly.
I know single vs double quotes, export, PATH, $(...) and $(( )).
I can write if/elif/else, [ ] vs [[ ]], file tests, case, and use exit codes.
I can loop over files and lines safely and use indexed and associative arrays.
I can write functions with local variables, return data with echo, and parse options with getopts.
I can process text with sed, awk, cut, tr, sort and uniq, including the top-10 pipeline.
I can use find with -name, -type, -mtime, -size, -exec and -delete safely.
I can use parameter expansion for paths and defaults, and create dates and temp files.
I can find and stop processes correctly (ps, pgrep, kill vs kill -9, nohup, jobs, trap).
I can schedule jobs with cron and write, check and read a systemd service.
I can find what fills the disk, check inodes, memory and load, and find deleted-but-open files.
I can check ports and services with ss, curl and nc, and debug DNS problems.
I can create SSH keys, fix their permissions, use ~/.ssh/config, and copy files with rsync.
I can pack and verify releases with tar and sha256sum, and install packages with apt.
I can troubleshoot: disk full, high CPU, port in use, service will not start, cannot SSH, DNS.
I start scripts with set -euo pipefail, clean up with trap, use locks, and keep scripts idempotent.
I can build a log analyzer, a backup with rotation, and a health check with alerts.
I can use jq, handle secrets safely, and test before reloading (nginx -t).
I can write CI steps: retry with backoff, wait for a port, git describe versions, deploy with rollback.
I can say each answer in 1-2 simple sentences, out loud, without notes.
